instructions: Listen to the presented audio clip while following along with the provided transcription. Record your own attempt at speaking the text, then play it back to compare with ours — re-record as many times as you need. This exercise also introduces alternate sound changes that may suit specific character choices, such as a pre-20th century period piece. As you go, fill out your blank Lexical Chart with the RP changes presented.

questions.text: Repeat After Me: Distinct Feature Tongue Twisters

items.note: If a syllable ending with rhoticity is followed by a syllable beginning with a vowel, that lost “R” colouring returns as a consonant “R” between the two. It helps to think of the “R” as starting the second word rather than ending the first.
items.sentence: The blurry star above appears either nearer or farther away depending on where I am.
items.ipa: /ðə blʌɹĭ stɑ ɹəbʌv əpɪə̆z aɪ̆ðə nɪɹə ɹɔ fɑðə ɹəweɪ̆ dəpɛndɪŋ ɒn wɛː ɹaɪ̆ æm/

items.note: An “R” inserts itself between a word ending in a vowel and one beginning with a vowel, even with no “R” in the spelling. It does not occur after a high vowel such as [i] or [u] — “the bee in the tree” keeps its gap, but “the claw in the paw” does not.
items.sentence: Krista is gaga over the drama of the conga on the dance floor.
items.ipa: /kɹɪstə ɹɪz gɑgɑ ɹəʊ̆və ðə dɹɑmə ɹəv ðə kɔŋgə ɹɒn ðə dɑns flɔ/

items.note: Present where [u] follows [t], [d], [n], [s], [z], the affricates [t͡ʃ] and [d͡ʒ], and rarely a light [l]. It relies partly on spelling: only in words spelled with “U” or occasionally “E-W”, never “O” or “OO” words like “too, zoo, soon”.
items.sentence: The only suitable meal while on duty on Tuesdays in June is a superbly chewy stew served with juice.
items.ipa: /ði əʊ̆nlĭ sɪ̆utəbɫ̩ miɫ waɪ̆ɫ ɒn dɪ̆utĭ ɒn ˈtɪ̆uzdeɪ̆z ɪn d͡ʒɪ̆un ɪz ə sɪ̆upɜblĭ t͡ʃɪ̆uwĭ stɪ̆u sɜvd wɪð d͡ʒɪ̆us/

items.note: Multisyllabic words ending in “-ury, -ory, -ary, -ery” lose the penultimate vowel. So “library” and “territory” become /ˈlaɪ̆bɹĭ/ and /ˈtɛɹɪˌtɹĭ/.
items.sentence: The observatory’s lavatory was inaccessible to the secretary in January and February.
items.ipa: /ði əbzɜvətɹĭz lævətɹĭ wəz ˌɪnɛkˈsɛsɪbɫ̩ tʊ ðə sɛkɹətɹĭ ɪn d͡ʒænjʊɹĭ ænd fɛbɹʊɹĭ/

items.note: The final syllable of “-ile” words takes equal stress, pronounced with the diphthong [aɪ̆] followed by a light [l].
items.sentence: The hostile juvenile was agile with his mobile phone.
items.ipa: /ðə hɒstaɪ̆l d͡ʒuvənaɪ̆l wəz æd͡ʒaɪ̆l wɪð hɪz məʊ̆baɪ̆l fəʊ̆n/

items.note: These changes read as more antiquated or upper class — most were present in Queen Elizabeth II’s idiolect. Not strictly “distinct features”, but grouped here as an example of that character.
items.sentence: It felt silly to worry about losing her way, for she had her map in her gray bag.
items.ipa: /ɪt fɛlt sɪlɪ tʊ wʌɾɪ əbaʊ̆t luzɪŋ hɜ wɛɪ̆ | fɔ ʃɪ hɛd hə mɛp ɪn hə gɾɛɪ̆ bɛg/
